chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 181 to 190, Ammuvanar's decade on the neythal flower: in every poem the blue lily of the shore appears, as the girls' eyes, a garland, a closing flower at evening, dawn bloom like a lover's eyes, or a flower cut down with the paddy, and the speakers move from the hope of marriage and the friend's disclosure to the heroine's grief and the eyes he heals or makes weep.

181.reading: The speaker says that if the lord of the shore, where unfailing girls with neythal-like eyes and lovely bamboo shoulders play sand games and set up the kuravai dance on heaps of white sand, would only grant his grace, living in this clamouring town would be sweet.
181.nuance: அழுங்கல் ஊர் is a town full of noise, and the noise is double: the girls' kuravai on the sand and the talk about her; one condition, நல்கின், would turn both into the sound of a wedding town.

thinai_evidence.note: the white sand of the ford and the shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the conditional நல்கின் and the complaint about the clamouring town fit the heroine wishing for marriage while the town talks

182.reading: The friend says that the one who struck this girl when she saw him at the great ford is no god of fearsome power but a man whose chest smells of a hand-woven garland of fragrant neythal mixed with cherunthi.
182.nuance: The household reads her sickness as a god's seizure (அணங்கு); the friend keeps the word but gives it a human subject, அணங்கியோன், and the garland is her evidence: a god would not wear a shore man's hand-made wreath.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal garland and the great ford of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; denying that a god caused the girl's sickness is the friend's disclosure of the affair (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்) to the foster mother

183.reading: Since the man who is lord of the land of falls and forests, of the small hills, of the town of good fields and of the cool sea has left her, the woman tells the helpless evening that it comes, unlike before, in the harsh daytime, as the neythal of the curved backwater closes, and that even when morning comes there is no one to take away her pain.
183.nuance: She gives him the titles of all four lands in a row, so the man has no landscape that is not his, while she has only the closing hour of the shore; and the last line refuses the usual comfort that night's end brings relief.

thinai_evidence.note: evening by the backwater, the shore's hour of lament

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine, after the man has left (பிரிந்தென), addresses the evening itself (மாலை, வருதி)

184.reading: The speaker says his town, where flocks of fish-eating herons leave the neythal of the dark backwater to rest in the seaside grove, is adorned by the sea, but greater than the sea is our friendship with him.
184.nuance: The sea is first his town's ornament, then the measure her love exceeds: the thing that most defines his place is the very thing she sets below their bond.

thinai_evidence.note: herons, seaside grove and the sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine affirms the bond (எமக்கு அவருடை நட்பே) against any doubt about the man of another shore town

185.reading: The man says the young girl at the front ford of Korkai of swaying-petalled neythal, with red lips set with teeth that shine like gleaming pearls and lovely saw-cut conch bangles, has speech as sweet as tuned lute strings.
185.nuance: Every ornament is a Korkai product: pearl from its sea, conch cut by the saw into bangles; the girl is described in the town's own wares, and only her voice needs an image from outside the shore.

thinai_evidence.note: neythal, the harbour ford and pearls

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the man describing the girl he has seen at the ford in the third person (குறுமகள் ... கிளவியளே) fits his telling his companion

186.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where women shake out their wet hair like a fine flock of herons, that their mother has said: a chariot comes many times to this ford where neythal drips on the swelling water, so do not go there.
186.nuance: The mother's sentence is quoted whole, so the hero hears the prohibition from the mother's own mouth; the chariot that betrays him is his own, and the visits it repeats (பல்கால்) are what ended them.

comparisons.tenor: women shaking out their wet hair

thinai_evidence.note: heron, neythal and the lord of the ford

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the friend addresses the hero as துறைவ and reports the mother's ban (என்றனள் யாயே), the confinement that urges marriage

187.reading: The friend tells the man that strangers do not accept these leaves: even the girls who come with us to bathe in the sea do not make dolls of the green-mixed neythal leaves, and for want of anyone to wear them on the body they carry only a few flowers set in a garland.
187.nuance: The 'these' of line 1 are best taken as the leaf garment the man offers as a courting gift; the friend refuses it by saying her company wears no stranger's leaves, so the refusal is also a reproach that he is still a நொதுமலாளர், a stranger, until he asks for her.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; refusing gifts from strangers (நொதுமலாளர் கொள்ளார் இவையே) fits the friend turning back the man's leaf gift

188.reading: The man says that his love's eyes have great beauty, like the neythal that opens at dawn at the great ford of Korkai of the lord of Korkai, where flocks of birds feed on red prawns of the dark backwater.
188.nuance: The flower is the dawn neythal, newly opened, not the evening one that closes (183); the time word makes the eyes fresh as well as blue.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns of the backwater and neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the man praising காதலி கண் in the third person speaks to himself or his companion

189.reading: The woman tells her friend that since the lord of the gentle shore, where the neythal dusted with fine punnai pollen looks as lovely as a gem set in gold, has come, her eyes have become good again.
189.nuance: The flower dusted with gold and the eyes made good are one image: her neythal-like eyes, grown pale in his absence, regain their colour as the blue flower takes on the punnai's gold.

thinai_evidence.note: punnai and neythal, the lord of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the heroine tells her friend (தோழி) that he has come (வந்தென), read as his coming to marry or his return

190.reading: The woman says that the lord of the gentle shore, where the reapers of white paddy cut down the fragrant cool neythal's opened white flower along with the grain, is surely the one who has made her many-petalled kohl eyes weep.
190.nuance: The reapers do not aim at the neythal; it falls because it grows among the paddy they want, so the harm in the image is careless, not cruel, and the eyes it spoils are named with the flower's own word, பல்லிதழ்.

comparisons.tenor: the man spoiling her flower-like eyes in passing

ullurai.tenor: the man and the woman whose eyes he has made weep

pairs.situation: her opened, flower-like eyes, named in line 4 by the flower's own word பல்லிதழ்
he harms her in passing, while about his own gain, not aiming at her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the neythal and the reapers of the fields beside her own shore town, things she knows (porul 7.26)

thinai_evidence.note: the weeping of the shore woman decides it, though the field things are marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; the woman names her own eyes (எம் பல்லிதழ் உண்கண்) and blames the man, as in a complaint to her friend

links.note: Kural 1150 says the town raises the very talk we want and the lover will grant (நல்குவர்) if he wishes; Ainkurunuru 181 says if the shore lord grants (நல்கின்), this clamouring town will be sweet to live in.
links.teaches: The Kural names the town's clamour as a lever that can push the lover to grant marriage, and the Ainkurunuru poem shows the far side of that lever: once he grants, the same noise becomes the festive kuravai of a town she can live in happily, so gossip and celebration are one sound judged before and after his word.

links.note: In Akananuru 272 the mother, seeing the garlanded lover at night, takes him for Murugu and worships; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend points to a garlanded chest and says he is no god of power.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems show the misreading the friend's disclosure has to undo: the household's habit of turning a garlanded young man into a god, which in Akananuru 272 leads to worship and in Ainkurunuru 182 is corrected by naming the garland as a shore man's hand-woven wreath.

links.note: In Natrinai 155 the hero on the neythal shore asks the girl whether she is a goddess of the sea; in Ainkurunuru 182 the friend says the one who struck the girl at the great ford is no god.
links.teaches: The belief that a beloved seen at the shore must be a divine power runs both ways, the man thinking her a sea goddess and the household thinking her stricken by a god, and in both the cure of the error is the same: the striker turns out to be a human lover who must be named.

links.note: Kural 1225's woman asks what good she has done the morning and what wrong the evening, so morning is the friendly hour; Ainkurunuru 183 ends that even if morning comes there is no one to clear her pain.
links.teaches: The Kural's separated woman still has a kind hour in the morning, while the Ainkurunuru heroine denies even that, so the pair shows two degrees of the same grief: one that rises and falls with the day, and one that the day's turn no longer touches.

links.note: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds in the morning, ripens through the day and blooms at evening; in Ainkurunuru 183 evening arrives early in the harsh day while the neythal of the backwater closes.
links.teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for evening pain gains a real flower in the Sangam poem, and the two move in opposite directions: as the shore's neythal closes at evening, the sickness opens, so the landscape's hour of rest is the lover's hour of full bloom of pain.

links.note: Kuruntokai 3's woman says her love for the hill man is larger than the earth, higher than the sky and deeper than the sea; Ainkurunuru 184's says the friendship with the man whose town the sea adorns is greater than the sea.
links.teaches: Each heroine measures love against her own lover's world: the hill woman needs the whole cosmos, while the shore woman takes the one thing that crowns his town and sets it below their bond, so the boast of measureless love takes its scale from the land of the man loved.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 185's man is taken by the Korkai girl's teeth bright as pearls; in Akananuru 27 the friend says the girl's red mouth with teeth like Korkai pearls may not hold the man who means to leave for wealth.
links.teaches: The pearl-toothed mouth of Korkai is what draws the man at first sight in Ainkurunuru 185 and what the friend in Akananuru 27 fears is not enough to keep him, so the same harbour formula marks both the start of the beauty's power and its limit against the call of wealth.

links.note: In Akananuru 20 the friend says mother, on the word of spiteful women, has confined the girl because a chariot circles the great ford day and night; in Ainkurunuru 186 the friend quotes mother herself saying a chariot comes often to this ford, so do not go.
links.teaches: In the long poem the confinement rests on the town's report, in the short one on the mother's own sight of the chariot, so the friend's warning to the lover can come in two strengths, and the second leaves him no excuse that it is only gossip.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 188's man compares his love's eyes to the neythal blooming at dawn at Korkai's great ford; in Natrinai 23 the friend says the girl's eyes have faded like the small-leaved neythal of Korkai's harbour.
links.teaches: The same Korkai neythal serves for the eyes in bloom when the lover praises them and for the eyes faded when the friend presses for marriage, so the flower's daily opening and closing lets one image carry both the courtship's first wonder and its later cost.

links.note: In 189 the lord of the gentle shore has come and her eyes have become good; in 190 the same மெல்லம் புலம்பன் is the one who made her many-petalled eyes weep.
links.teaches: Placed side by side in the decade with the same name for the man, the two poems make the heroine's eyes a gauge wholly in his hands, healed by his coming and wet by his absence, and the neythal image follows them, dusted with gold in one and cut down in the other.

links.note: In 170 a small white gull tears the neythal of the backwater, and the friend is asked why the eyes of one with such a good man grow pale; in 190 reapers cut down the neythal flower while harvesting white paddy, and the man has made her eyes weep.
links.teaches: Both hide the spoiled eyes in a destroyed neythal, but the destroyers differ: the gull tears it to feed, the reapers fell it only because it stands among the grain they want, so the decade offers two kinds of blame, appetite and indifference, for the same harm.

links.note: Kural 1171's woman asks why her eyes weep when it was they who showed him to her; Ainkurunuru 190's woman says the lord of the shore surely is the one who made her eyes weep.
links.teaches: For the same tears the Kural's woman blames her own eyes for having looked, while the Ainkurunuru woman blames the man with an emphatic மன்ற, so the pair shows the two directions in which the abandoned lover can turn the fault, inward on her own seeing or outward on him.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem and says so in its note.
187 is obscure: what இவை (line 1) refers to and the sense of உடலகம் கொள்வோர் (line 4) are not fixed by the text; read as the friend refusing a leaf gift, marked uncertain.
